findings.reason: The protected Python solution implements a SparseVector using a hash map storing only nonzero index-value pairs. During dotProduct, it iterates over the smaller map and queries the larger map in expected O(1) time per nonzero entry. Construction takes O(N) time and O(K1 + K2) space, while dotProduct takes O(min(K1, K2)) time. The implementation is expert quality; no candidate is required.
Filtering out zeros during initialization leaves only coordinates that can contribute a non-zero product. Swapping smaller and larger maps ensures dotProduct probes the map with fewer keys.
Scanning N elements takes O(N) time. Intersecting nonzeros takes O(min(K1, K2)) time with O(K1 + K2) total auxiliary space. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts dense vectors nums1 and nums2, constructing SparseVector objects and returning the exact integer dot product sum.

The approach accurately details nonzero coordinate map storage, smaller-map lookup probing, dot product sum calculation, and O(N + min(K1, K2)) time / O(K1 + K2) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover sorted index-value pairs, dense coordinate zip scanning, pairwise sparse matching overhead, all-zero vectors, disjoint supports, single shared nonzeros, dense vector degradation, and equal dimensions.
